issue: Double "then" in consecutive sentences ("It is evident, then, ... How, then,"); source has "it is evident" only once and no second "then".
replacement: The people are the only legitimate fountain of power, and the constitutional charter under which the separate branches of government hold their power is derived from them. It therefore seems entirely consistent with republican theory to return to that same original authority, not only whenever the powers of the government need to be enlarged, reduced or remodeled, but also whenever any one of the departments encroaches on the chartered authorities of the others. The separate departments are perfectly co-ordinate under the terms of their common commission. It is evident that none of them can claim an exclusive or superior right to settle the boundaries between their respective powers. How, then, are the encroachments of the stronger to be prevented, or the wrongs of the weaker to be redressed, without an appeal to the people themselves? As the grantors of the commissions, they alone can declare its true meaning and enforce its observance.

issue: Source concedes a premise: "If it be true that all governments rest on opinion, it is no less true that...". Candidate "It may be true that all governments rest on opinion. It is no less true that..." turns the concession into a hedge ("may be").
replacement: In the next place, there is an objection that may be considered inherent in the principle. Every appeal to the people would carry an implication that the government has some defect. Frequent appeals would therefore, to a great extent, deprive the government of the veneration that time bestows on everything, and without which even the wisest and freest governments would perhaps lack the stability they require. If it is true that all governments rest on opinion, it is no less true that the strength of opinion in each individual, and its practical influence on his conduct, depend greatly on the number of others he supposes to have held the same opinion. The reason of man, like man himself, is timid and cautious when left alone, and gains firmness and confidence in proportion to the number with which it is associated. When the examples that fortify opinion are ANCIENT as well as NUMEROUS, they are known to have a double effect. In a nation of philosophers this consideration ought to be disregarded, because the voice of enlightened reason would be enough to instill a reverence for the laws. But a nation of philosophers is as little to be expected as the philosophical race of kings that Plato wished for. And in every other nation, even the most rational government will find it no superfluous advantage to have the prejudices of the community on its side.

issue: Separation-of-powers vocabulary: source "a very feeble RESTRAINT on power" (and "restraints of the Constitution"); candidate renders the first as "check", importing a term the source does not use at this point.
replacement: Note that in examining these expedients I confine myself to how well they would ENFORCE the Constitution by keeping the separate departments of power within their proper bounds. I am not considering them in particular as ways of ALTERING the Constitution itself. Looked at in the first way, appeals to the people at fixed periods seem almost as unsuitable as appeals on particular occasions, as these arise. Suppose the periods are separated by short intervals. Then the measures to be reviewed and corrected will be recent, and will be tangled up with all the circumstances that tend to corrupt and distort the result of occasional revisions. Suppose the periods are far apart. Then the same remark applies to all recent measures. And whatever advantage the distance of the older measures may give to a dispassionate review of them comes with drawbacks that seem to outweigh it. In the first place, a distant prospect of public censure would be a very feeble restraint on power when present motives drive it to excess. Can anyone imagine that a legislative assembly of a hundred or two hundred members, eagerly bent on some favorite object and breaking through the restraints of the Constitution to reach it, would be stopped by the thought that its conduct would be reviewed by a censorial body ten, fifteen or twenty years from now? In the next place, the abuses would often have done their harm before the remedy was applied. And in the last place, where that might not be so, the abuses would be of long standing, would have taken deep root, and would not easily be pulled out.

issue: Source: "the necessary partition of power among the several departments, as laid down in the Constitution". Candidate drops "necessary" and turns "as laid down in" into "that the Constitution requires" (stronger claim).
replacement: What expedient, then, shall we finally turn to for keeping up in practice the necessary partition of power among the separate departments, as laid down in the Constitution? The only possible answer is this. All these external provisions have proved inadequate, so the gap must be filled by designing the interior structure of the government in such a way that its separate parts, through their relations with one another, serve to keep each other in their proper places. I will not presume to develop this important idea in full. But I will venture a few general observations that may perhaps put it in a clearer light and help us judge more accurately the principles and structure of the government the Convention has planned.

issue: Style note keeps "separate and distinct" in Nos. 47-51; candidate recasts as adverbs "separately and distinctly".
replacement: Everyone admits that, to a certain extent, a separate and distinct exercise of the different powers of government is essential to the preservation of liberty. To lay a proper foundation for that, each department plainly needs a will of its own. Each must therefore be constituted so that its members have as little part as possible in appointing the members of the others. Followed strictly, this principle would require that every appointment to the supreme executive, legislative and judiciary offices be drawn from the same fountain of authority, the people, through channels with no communication whatever between them. Perhaps such a plan for constructing the separate departments would be less difficult in practice than it may seem to be in contemplation. Still, some difficulties, and some added expense, would come with carrying it out. Some departures from the principle must therefore be allowed. In constituting the judiciary department in particular, it might be unwise to insist strictly on the principle. First, since peculiar qualifications are essential in its members, the main concern ought to be to choose the mode of selection that best secures those qualifications. Secondly, the permanent tenure by which judges hold their appointments must soon destroy any sense of dependence on the authority that conferred them.

issue: Source: "the necessary constitutional means and personal motives"; candidate drops "necessary".
replacement: But the great security against a gradual concentration of the several powers in one department is to give those who run each department the necessary constitutional means and the personal motives to resist encroachments by the others. Here, as everywhere, the provision for defense must be made proportionate to the danger of attack. Ambition must be made to counteract ambition. The interest of the man must be tied to the constitutional rights of the place. It may be a reflection on human nature that such devices are needed to control the abuses of government. But what is government itself but the greatest of all reflections on human nature? If men were angels, no government would be necessary. If angels were to govern men, neither external nor internal controls on government would be necessary. In framing a government to be administered by men over men, the great difficulty lies in this: you must first enable the government to control the governed, and then oblige it to control itself. A dependence on the people is, no doubt, the primary control on the government; but experience has taught mankind that auxiliary precautions are necessary.

issue: Source: "As the weight of the legislative authority requires that it should be thus divided, the weakness of the executive may require, on the other hand, that it should be fortified." Candidate "The legislative authority is heavy, and that requires it to be divided" mistranslates "weight" (preponderance) as literal heaviness and loses the as/so link. Also the leading question "May not this defect of an absolute negative be supplied by..." is flattened to a neutral "Could ... ?" plus a statement.
replacement: But it is impossible to give every department an equal power of self-defense. In republican government the legislative authority necessarily predominates. The remedy for this problem is to divide the legislature into different branches. These should be made as little connected with each other as the nature of their common functions and their common dependence on the society will permit, by giving them different modes of election and different principles of action. It may even be necessary to guard against dangerous encroachments with still further precautions. Because the weight of the legislative authority requires that it be divided in this way, the weakness of the executive may require, on the other hand, that it be strengthened. An absolute negative on the legislature appears, at first view, to be the natural defense with which to arm the chief executive. But perhaps it would be neither entirely safe nor sufficient by itself. On ordinary occasions it might not be used with the needed firmness, and on extraordinary occasions it might be treacherously abused. May not this lack of an absolute negative be made up by some qualified connection between this weaker department and the weaker branch of the stronger department, by which that branch may be led to support the constitutional rights of the executive without being too much detached from the rights of its own department?

issue: Source: "the insecurity of rights ... would be displayed by such reiterated oppressions of factious majorities THAT some power altogether independent of the people would soon be called for by the voice of the very factions whose misrule had proved the necessity of it." Candidate rewrites the such...that result clause as "Factional majorities would oppress again and again, until the very factions ... would soon be calling for", which is ungrammatical ("until ... soon") and makes the factions' call a terminus rather than a result.
replacement: Second. In a republic it matters greatly not only to guard the society against the oppression of its rulers but to guard one part of the society against the injustice of the other part. Different classes of citizens necessarily have different interests. If a majority is united by a common interest, the rights of the minority will be insecure. There are only two ways to provide against this evil. One is to create a will in the community that is independent of the majority, that is, independent of the society itself. The other is to include in the society so many separate kinds of citizens that an unjust combination of a majority of the whole becomes very improbable, if not impossible. The first way is the one found in all governments that hold an hereditary or self-appointed authority. At best this is a precarious security, because a power independent of the society may as readily take up the unjust views of the majority as the rightful interests of the minority, and may even be turned against both parties. The second way will be exemplified in the federal republic of the United States. All authority in it will be derived from the society and dependent on it, while the society itself will be broken into so many parts, interests and classes of citizens that the rights of individuals, or of the minority, will be in little danger from self-interested combinations of the majority. In a free government the security for civil rights must be the same as that for religious rights. In the one case it consists in the multiplicity of interests, and in the other in the multiplicity of sects. In both cases the degree of security will depend on the number of interests and sects, and this may be presumed to depend on the extent of country and the number of people brought under the same government. This view of the subject must particularly recommend a proper federal system to all the sincere and thoughtful friends of republican government. It shows that to the exact degree that the territory of the Union may be formed into smaller Confederacies or States, oppressive combinations of a majority will be made easier. The best security that the republican forms offer for the rights of every class of citizens will then be weakened. And so the stability and independence of some member of the government, the only other security, must be increased in the same proportion. Justice is the end of government. It is the end of civil society. It always has been, and always will be, pursued until it is obtained, or until liberty is lost in the pursuit. Take a society organized in such a way that the stronger faction can readily unite and oppress the weaker. Anarchy may as truly be said to reign there as in a state of nature, where the weaker individual has no protection against the violence of the stronger. And in the state of nature even the stronger individuals are driven by the uncertainty of their condition to accept a government that can protect the weak as well as themselves. In the same way, in the former case the more powerful factions or parties will gradually be led by a like motive to want a government that will protect all parties, the weaker as well as the more powerful. It can hardly be doubted that if the State of Rhode Island were separated from the Confederacy and left to itself, the insecurity of rights under popular government within such narrow limits would be displayed by such repeated oppressions by factional majorities that some power altogether independent of the people would soon be called for by the voice of the very factions whose misrule had proved the need for it. In the extended republic of the United States, with the great variety of interests, parties and sects that it embraces, a coalition of a majority of the whole society could seldom form on any principles other than those of justice and the general good. And since a minority would thus have less to fear from the will of a majority, there would also be less pretext for providing for its security by bringing into the government a will not dependent on the majority, or, in other words, a will independent of the society itself. It is as certain as it is important, whatever contrary opinions have been held, that the larger the society, provided it lies within a practical sphere, the better able it will be to govern itself. And happily for the REPUBLICAN CAUSE, the practicable sphere may be carried to a very great extent by a judicious modification and mixture of the FEDERAL PRINCIPLE.

issue: Source: "as dissatisfactory to some of the States as it would have been difficult to the convention"; candidate "burdened the Convention" changes "difficult".
replacement: The first thing to examine in this part of the government is the qualifications of the electors and of the elected. The electors are to have the same qualifications as those who elect the most numerous branch of the State legislatures. The definition of the right of suffrage is very justly regarded as a fundamental article of republican government, so the Convention was bound to define and establish this right in the Constitution. To leave it open to occasional regulation by Congress would have been improper, for the reason just given. To leave it to the legislative discretion of the States would have been improper for the same reason. It would also have made too dependent on the State governments a branch of the federal government that ought to depend on the people alone. To reduce the different qualifications in the different States to one uniform rule would probably have displeased some of the States as much as it would have been difficult for the Convention. The provision the Convention made therefore appears to be the best of the choices open to it. It must satisfy every State, because it conforms to the standard that the State itself has already established, or may establish. It will be safe for the United States because, being fixed by the State constitutions, it cannot be altered by the State governments; and there is no reason to fear that the people of the States will alter this part of their constitutions so as to cut down the rights the federal Constitution secures to them.

issue: Addition. Source: "without regard to poverty or wealth, or to any particular profession of religious faith". Candidate "and of any religious faith or none in particular" adds "or none" (a claim about persons of no faith the source does not make).
replacement: The State constitutions define the qualifications of the elected less carefully and properly, and these qualifications are also better suited to uniformity. The Convention has therefore very properly considered and regulated them itself. A representative of the United States must be twenty-five years old, must have been a citizen of the United States for seven years, must be an inhabitant of the State he is to represent at the time of his election, and must hold no office under the United States while he serves. Under these reasonable limits, the door to this part of the federal government stands open to merit of every description, whether native or adoptive, young or old, poor or rich, and without regard to any particular profession of religious faith.

issue: Source is a parallel "As it is essential... so it is particularly essential"; candidate makes the second half an inference ("It therefore requires").
replacement: First. Liberty requires that the government in general have a common interest with the people, and it requires in particular that the branch we are considering depend directly on the people and feel close sympathy with them. Frequent elections are without question the only policy that can effectively secure this dependence and sympathy. But how frequent they must be to do it cannot, it seems, be calculated exactly, and depends on a variety of circumstances connected with the matter. Let us consult experience, the guide that ought always to be followed whenever it can be found.

issue: (a) Source: "being at most but very imperfectly known to ancient polity" (forms of government); candidate "Ancient politics knew" changes the referent. (b) Source keeps a conditional: "And if we may argue from the degree of liberty retained even under septennial elections, and all the other vicious ingredients ..., we cannot doubt that..."; candidate drops "if we may argue" and substitutes an added imperative "Now consider ... From this we cannot doubt".
replacement: Ancient forms of government knew the scheme of representation, as a substitute for a meeting of the citizens in person, only very imperfectly at best. We should therefore expect instructive examples only from more modern times. Even among these, to avoid a search too vague and sprawling, we should limit ourselves to the few examples that are best known and most closely resemble our own case. The first one that fits this description is the House of Commons in Great Britain. The history of this branch of the English Constitution before Magna Charta is too obscure to teach anything. Students of political antiquities have even questioned whether it existed. The earliest records from after that date show only that parliaments were to SIT every year, not that they were to be ELECTED every year. Even these annual sessions were left so much to the monarch's discretion that royal ambition, under various pretexts, often arranged very long and dangerous gaps between them. To remedy this grievance, a statute in the reign of Charles II provided that the gaps should not be stretched beyond three years. When William III came to the throne and a revolution took place in the government, the subject was taken up again, more seriously, and it was declared to be among the fundamental rights of the people that parliaments ought to be held FREQUENTLY. Another statute, passed a few years later in the same reign, gave the word "frequently," which had referred to the three-year period fixed under Charles II, a precise meaning: it expressly enacted that a new parliament must be called within three years after the end of the previous one. The last change, from three years to seven, is well known to have come fairly early in the present century, under an alarm for the Hanoverian succession. These facts show that the greatest frequency of elections ever thought necessary in that kingdom to bind the representatives to their constituents is no more than a return every three years. And if we may argue from the degree of liberty that survives even under septennial elections and all the other vicious ingredients in the parliamentary constitution, we cannot doubt that cutting the period from seven years to three, together with the other needed reforms, would extend the people's influence over their representatives enough to satisfy us that biennial elections under the federal system cannot possibly endanger the dependence the House of Representatives must have on its constituents.

issue: Source: "the means of influence over the popular branch possessed by the other BRANCHES of the government above cited" (the permanent branches of the British and other cited governments). Candidate "the other governments I have cited possessed" drops "branches" and changes who holds the means.
replacement: Three further circumstances considerably strengthen the conclusion these examples lead to. The first is that the federal legislature will hold only a part of the supreme legislative authority that is vested entirely in the British Parliament, and that the colonial assemblies and the Irish legislature, with a few exceptions, exercised. It is a received and well-founded maxim that, other things being equal, the greater the power, the shorter its duration ought to be; and conversely, the smaller the power, the more safely its duration may be extended. In the second place, it has been shown elsewhere that the federal legislature will be restrained by its dependence on its people, as other legislative bodies are, and will also be watched and controlled by the collateral legislatures of the individual States, which other legislative bodies are not. And in the third place, there is no comparison between the means the more permanent branches of the federal government will have to seduce the House of Representatives from its duty to the people, if they were disposed to try, and the means of influence over the popular branch that the other branches of the governments I have cited possessed. With less power to abuse, therefore, the federal representatives can be less tempted on one side, and will be doubly watched on the other.

issue: Source: "we find them by no means coinciding any more in this instance, than in the elections of other civil magistrates." Candidate "They differ here no more than they do" drops "by no means" and can be read as "they differ only slightly". Also source "either the one or the other of these States" (two States) is rendered "any of these States".
replacement: I shall perhaps be reminded here of a common saying, "that where annual elections end, tyranny begins." It has often been remarked that sayings that become proverbs are generally founded in reason. It is no less true that, once they are established, they are often applied to cases the reason behind them does not reach. The case before us is proof enough. What is the reason this proverb is founded on? No one will expose himself to ridicule by pretending that there is any natural connection between the sun or the seasons and the length of time human virtue can stand up to the temptations of power. Happily for mankind, liberty is not tied to any single point of time in this respect. It lies between extremes that leave room for all the variations that the different situations and circumstances of civil society may require. The election of public officials might be daily, weekly or monthly, as well as annual, if that were found expedient; in some instances it actually has been. And if circumstances may call for a departure from the rule in one direction, why not in the other? Look at the periods established among ourselves for electing the most numerous branches of the State legislatures. They by no means coincide here, any more than in the elections of other civil officials. In Connecticut and Rhode Island the periods are half-yearly. In the other States, except South Carolina, they are annual. In South Carolina they are biennial, as is proposed for the federal government. That is a difference of four to one between the longest and shortest periods. Yet it would not be easy to show that Connecticut or Rhode Island is better governed, or enjoys more rational liberty, than South Carolina. Nor would it be easy to show that either of these States is distinguished in those respects, or by those causes, from the States whose elections differ from both.

issue: Changed claim. Source: "who will pretend that the liberties of the people of America will NOT BE MORE secure under biennial elections, unalterably fixed by such a Constitution, than those of any other nation would be". Candidate "will be LESS secure" is a different (weaker) proposition: the source asserts the American people will be MORE secure; the candidate only denies they will be less secure. Also "fixing the national sentiment" keeps the archaic sense of "sentiment" (style note: feelings).
replacement: I can find only one ground for this doctrine, and it is wholly inapplicable to our case. Americans understand well the important distinction between a Constitution established by the people and unalterable by the government, and a law established by the government and alterable by the government. In any other country this distinction seems to have been little understood and less observed. Wherever the supreme power of legislation has resided, people have supposed that it also held a full power to change the form of the government. Even in Great Britain, where the principles of political and civil liberty have been most discussed and where we hear most about the rights of the Constitution, it is maintained that the authority of Parliament is transcendent and uncontrollable, as much over the Constitution as over the ordinary objects of legislation. Parliament has accordingly, in several instances, changed some of the most fundamental articles of the government by legislative acts. In particular, it has several times changed the period of election. On the last occasion it not only brought in septennial elections in place of triennial ones, but in the same act extended its own term four years beyond what the people had elected it for. Attention to these dangerous practices has naturally alarmed the devotees of free government, of which frequent elections are the cornerstone, and has led them to look for some security for liberty against the danger it faces. Where no Constitution paramount to the government existed or could be had, no constitutional security like the one established in the United States could be tried. Some other security had to be found. What better security would the case allow than to pick some simple and familiar portion of time and appeal to it as a standard, by which to measure the danger of innovations, to fix the national feeling and to unite patriotic efforts? The simplest and most familiar portion of time suited to the purpose was a year. Hence a laudable zeal, seeking to put up some barrier against the gradual innovations of an unlimited government, has taught the doctrine that the approach of tyranny can be measured by how far one departs from the fixed point of annual elections. But what need is there to apply this expedient to a government limited, as the federal government will be, by the authority of a paramount Constitution? Or who will claim that the liberties of the people of America will not be more secure under biennial elections, unalterably fixed by such a Constitution, than those of any other nation would be where elections were annual, or even more frequent, but could be altered by the ordinary power of the government?

issue: Awkward "Even so, so large a part"; source is one concessive "whatever improvements may be suggested by experience... so great a portion of a year would elapse".
replacement: Our frequent elections have advantages, even in single States, but mixed in with them is a drawback. Where the States are large and hold only one legislative session a year, spurious elections cannot be investigated and annulled in time for the decision to have its proper effect. If a man can get a return, no matter by what unlawful means, the irregular member takes his seat as a matter of course and is sure to hold it long enough to serve his purposes. Hence a very harmful encouragement is given to using unlawful means to get irregular returns. If elections for the federal legislature were annual, this practice might become a very serious abuse, particularly in the more distant States. Each house is, as it necessarily must be, the judge of the elections, qualifications and returns of its members. However many improvements experience may suggest for simplifying and speeding up the process in disputed cases, so large a part of a year would unavoidably pass before an illegitimate member could be removed from his seat that the prospect of it would do little to check unfair and illicit means of getting a seat.

issue: Source paraphrases the Constitution's ineligibility clause: "or of which the emoluments may be increased". STYLE-NOTE keeps "emolument" in a direct reference to the clause and requires paraphrases of legal text to keep the key terms; candidate has "whose pay may be increased". (Own-prose "emoluments of office" -> "pay" earlier in the paragraph is correct.)
replacement: Is the danger feared from the other branches of the federal government? But where will the President, or the Senate, or both, find the means? Their pay for office, it is to be presumed, will not exceed what is needed for very different purposes, and without first corrupting the House of Representatives it cannot. Their private fortunes, since they must all be American citizens, cannot possibly be sources of danger. The only means they can have, then, lie in handing out appointments. Is it here that suspicion rests her charge? Sometimes we are told that the President is to use up this fund of corruption in subduing the virtue of the Senate. Now it is the fidelity of the other House that is to be the victim. The improbability of such a mercenary and treacherous combination among the several members of the government should alone quiet this fear. They stand on foundations as different as republican principles will well allow, and they are at the same time accountable to the society over which they are placed. But fortunately the Constitution has provided a still further safeguard. The members of Congress are made ineligible to any civil offices that may be created, or whose emoluments may be increased, during the term for which they were elected. No offices, therefore, can be handed out to the sitting members except those that fall vacant by ordinary chance. To suppose that these would be enough to buy the guardians of the people, chosen by the people themselves, is to give up every rule by which events ought to be calculated, and to put in its place an indiscriminate and unbounded jealousy, against which all reasoning must be useless. The sincere friends of liberty who surrender themselves to the extravagances of this passion do not realize the injury they do their own cause. There is a degree of depravity in mankind that calls for a certain degree of caution and distrust; but there are other qualities in human nature that justify a certain portion of esteem and confidence. Republican government presupposes these qualities in a higher degree than any other form does. If the pictures that the political jealousy of some among us has drawn were faithful likenesses of the human character, the inference would be that men do not have enough virtue for self-government, and that nothing less than the chains of despotism can keep them from destroying and devouring one another.
